catalog_quote: [p.30] L'accent de la langue touarègue n'est connu que dans ses grandes lignes. [...] C'est essentiellement un accent musical avec des variations dynamiques peu prononcées. [...] c) La place de l'accent principal et l'espèce de rythme exigée paraît dépendre de la structure syllabique quantitative de chaque unité accentuelle, mais de façon assez compliquée [...] L'accent n'a donc pas de fonction phonologique. Il n'existe pas de paires de mots qui se distinguent uniquement par (la place de) l'accent. [p.31] h) Les syllabes longues, et par conséquent les voyelles longues, attirent sans doute dans certaines limites l'accent principal. [p.32] 2) L'accent des mots isolés. [...] a) Le rythme creux avec l'accent sur l'antépénultième est exigé par: (1) Les noms trisyllabiques au sing. qui ont la pénult. brève ou fermée par une gém. et se terminent sur voyelle, p.ex.: áġənnà „ciel" [...] c) Le rythme égal avec l'accent sur la pénultième est exigé par: (1) Tous les noms sg. ou pl. de 3 syllabes ou moins, exceptés ceux du § a, p.ex.: ekábăr „hutte" [...] [p.33] (2) Tous les verbes de 3 syllabes ou moins sans voyelle longue exceptés certains du § d(3) et ceux du § a(4) [...] d) Le rythme égal avec l'accent sur l'antépénultième est exigé par: (1) Les noms de plus de 3 syllabes, l'antépénultième étant de quantité longue [...] f) Le rythme égal avec l'accent sur la dernière syllabe est exigé par: (1) Les noms de nombre 1-10 masculins.

sweep_summary: taha1241 (Tahaggart Tamahaq) is not in the catalog. The single title-works with stress in the title, Aikhenvald & Nientao 1988 'On accent in Tamasheq' (Russian, 3 pp., Moscow postgraduate conference volume), is confirmed to exist by Aikhenvald's own CV (saved:, p.24) but no copy or abstract is reachable online; its variety is unclear (the Russian 'tamashek' is generic Tuareg and the Malian co-author suggests Mali Tamasheq, taq, rather than Ahaggar), so relevance is unclear and acquisition priority medium (print only in Russia). The best first-hand statement actually read is Prasse 1972, Manuel de grammaire touaregue (tahaggart), pp. 30-37 (already held by the project, page scan verified against the scanned): a non-contrastive pitch accent, penultimate by default for nouns/verbs of <=3 syllables, antepenultimate for trisyllabic nouns with light or geminate-closed penult ending in a vowel and for plural types 2/3/4/7 (Ahaggar and Aïr, not Iwellemmeden), final for masculine numerals and long-final intensive perfects, with many rules flagged as provisional. Vycichl & Chaker 1984 (Encyclopédie berbère 'Accent') is a consistent second-hand summary of Prasse. only direct downloads and APIs were used. updated (addendum).

new_statements.translation: [p.30] The place of the main accent and the kind of rhythm required appear to depend on the quantitative syllable structure of each accentual unit, but in a rather complicated way [...] Accent therefore has no phonological function. There are no pairs of words distinguished solely by (the place of) the accent. [p.32] a) 'Hollow rhythm' with accent on the antepenult is required by: (1) trisyllabic singular nouns whose penult is short or closed by a geminate and which end in a vowel, e.g. áġənnà 'sky' [...] c) 'Even rhythm' with accent on the penult is required by: (1) all nouns, sg. or pl., of 3 syllables or fewer, except those of § a [...] [p.33] (2) all verbs of 3 syllables or fewer without a long vowel [...]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tahaggart has a non-contrastive, mainly musical (pitch) word accent. In isolated words the main accent falls on the penult by default for nouns and verbs of up to three syllables; it retracts to the antepenult under quantity/morphological conditions (trisyllabic sg. nouns with light or geminate-closed penult ending in a vowel, penult closed by a geminate, certain plural classes, nouns of >3 syllables with a long antepenult, verbs with long antepenult vowel); intensive verb forms accent their first long vowel; masculine numerals 1-10 and a few verb forms with long final vowel are final-accented. In enclitic groups the accent tends to shift to the syllable adjacent to the clitic. Prasse stresses the rules are provisional ('n'est connu que dans ses grandes lignes').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees distinguished: principal (high tone, slight dynamic increase), secondary (mid tone), tertiary (low tone); normal 'rythme égal' rises to the main accent and falls after it (3-2-1-2-3), while 'rythme creux' places a tertiary syllable adjacent to the main accent (2-3-1-3-2); Prasse marks principal with acute and tertiary with grave (e.g. áġənnà).
new_statements.exceptions: Numerals 1-10 masc. final (əssín, səmmús); kălá 'non' final; intensive perfects accent the long vowel (iktâb final); dialect differences: Y follows Ahaggar for plurals like íkəbrân but WE/WW/N say ikə́brân; several sub-rules explicitly marked 'sujette à des vérifications ultérieures'; possible accent displacement under emphasis (p.37).
new_statements.domain_note: Rules stated for 'mots autonomes à l'état isolé' (citation forms); the accentual unit may be a word or an enclitic group with one main accent, with separate rules (§B.3, pp. 34-37) for accent placement and shift in enclitic groups; accent is independent of poetic metre, which is quantity-based.
new_statements.identity_note: Prasse 1972 describes the tăhăggart dialect (Kel-Ahaggar, Tamanrasset), i.e. exactly taha1241, based mainly on Foucauld's Ahaggar materials plus Prasse's own 1958 notes; he flags dialect differences in accent for Y (Ayer), WE/WW (Tawellemmet, Niger/Mali) and N, which are other glottocodes (e.g. tama1365 Tamasheq, tawa1286/ayer varieties) and should not be conflated.

[...] The accent therefore has no phonological function; there are no word pairs distinguished solely by (the position of) the accent. [...] (a) The 'hollow rhythm' with accent on the antepenult is required by: (1) trisyllabic singular nouns whose penult is short or closed by a geminate and which end in a vowel [...] (c) The 'even rhythm' with accent on the penult is required by: (1) all nouns, sg. or pl., of 3 syllables or fewer, except those under (a).
new_statements.citation: Prasse, Karl-G. 1972. Manuel de grammaire touaregue (tahaggart), I-III: Phonetique - Ecriture - Pronom. Copenhague: Akademisk Forlag, pp. 30-33 (Ch. I, B 'L'accent', 1 Généralités; 2 L'accent des mots isolés).
new_statements.reading: Tahaggart word accent is a non-contrastive pitch accent whose position is predictable from syllable quantity and morphological class: default penultimate (nouns and long-vowel-less verbs of <=3 syllables), antepenultimate when the penult is light/geminate-closed and the word ends in a vowel, in several plural types (Ahaggar/Aïr-specific), and in longer nouns with a heavy antepenult; final in masculine numerals 1-10 and in intensive perfects with a long final vowel; intensives accent the first lengthened vowel; clitic groups re-align accent. Prasse himself flags the polysyllable rules as provisional. For a catalog's classification this is a quantity-sensitive, morphologically conditioned system with penultimate as the unmarked position, not a fixed-position system.

new_statements.quote: [p. 148] La voyelle variable du parfait est la voy.carac. comme à la cj.I. Au pf.int. elle est surlongue (f,Q,3) et accentuée, au pf. simple elle est longue et non accentuée. [p. 182] Malgré cette restriction morphologique les pf. simple et int. se distinguent cependant nettement aux deux nombres à l'aide de l'accent. Le pf. simple a l'accent à l'antépénultième, le pf.int. à la pénultième, p.ex.: âlos wa bähäwän/middän wi báhawnîn (déf.). alos bähäwän/middän bähäwnîn (indéf.). Le phénomène est probablement dû au fait que les vocalisations á-à et å-a ne distinguaient pas primitivement les deux pf.
new_statements.translation: [p. 148] The variable vowel of the perfect is the characteristic vowel, as in conjugation I. In the intensive perfect it is overlong and accented; in the simple perfect it is long and unaccented. [p. 182] Despite this morphological restriction, the simple and intensive perfects are nonetheless clearly distinguished in both numbers by means of the accent. The simple perfect has the accent on the antepenult, the intensive perfect on the penult, e.g. âlos wa bähäwän / middän wi báhawnîn (definite); alos bähäwän / middän bähäwnîn (indefinite). The phenomenon is probably due to the fact that the vocalisations á-à and å-a did not originally distinguish the two perfects.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The verb volume has no accent chapter (the accent section is in vol. I, 1972); it only makes two scattered remarks: the overlong characteristic vowel of the intensive perfect carries the accent, while the merely long vowel of the simple perfect does not (p. 148), and in conjugation IV participles the simple perfect is accented on the antepenult and the intensive perfect on the penult (p. 182). new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the p. 182 pattern is itself a morphologically conditioned contrast (antepenult in pf. simple participles vs penult in pf. intensif participles). The scanned string '(f,Q,3)' is a mangled cross-reference, kept verbatim.
new_statements.identity_note: All works are about the Ahaggar (Hoggar) variety: Prasse's Manuel is explicitly 'tăhăggart' and flags where its accent rules do not hold for southern dialects (Aïr/Y keeps rule a(3); Iwellemmeden WE/WW and N do not; the WE of the Kel-Aghlal accent the antepenult in the simple perfect); Motylinski states on p. 2 that the Hoggar dialect is called tamahaq by its speakers and on p. 6 lists Hoggar, Ifor'as, Adhar', Azger, Ahir and Aoulimiden as differing dialects; Hanoteau's grammar is based on Imouchar' consultants in Algiers in 1858 and is filed under Tahaggart (thv) by the MPI record.

new_statements.rule_in_words: A non-contrastive, essentially musical (pitch) accent whose position depends on the quantitative syllable structure of the accentual unit. Isolated words: penult by default (all nouns of three syllables or fewer; verbs of three syllables or fewer without a long vowel; intensive verbs with a long penult); antepenult ('rythme creux') for trisyllabic nouns with a light or geminate-closed penult and a final vowel, for plural types 2, 3, 4 and 7, for trisyllabic verbs with a geminate onset of the final syllable, and for trisyllabic independent pronouns; pre-antepenult only in quadrisyllabic feminine plural pronouns. Long syllables attract the main accent within limits. Enclitic groups form one accentual unit and the accent moves to the syllable adjacent to the other member of the group.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three accent levels: principal (high tone, slight dynamic increase), secondary (mid tone), tertiary (low tone). Normal rhythm rises to the main accent and falls after it (3-2-1-2-3); the 'rythme creux' puts a tertiary-accent syllable next to the main accent (2-3-1-3-2). In enclitic groups a word that loses the main accent keeps a secondary accent on the syllable that would carry it in isolation.
new_statements.exceptions: Rules a(2) and a(4) and c(2) are flagged as needing further verification; rule a(2) may not hold for nouns with a short characteristic vowel; rule a(3) holds for Aïr (Y) but not for WE, WW, N (ikébrân, ihänân); for the WE of the Kel-Aghlal the antepenult is accented unless the penult has the overlong vowel of an intensive perfect; verb + suffix pronoun t/tt or particle d/dd groups are accented as if the clitic were absent; enclitic-group placement cannot yet be given by simple rules.
new_statements.identity_note: All works are about the Ahaggar (Hoggar) variety: Prasse's Manuel is explicitly 'tăhăggart' and flags where its accent rules do not hold for southern dialects (Aïr/Y keeps rule a(3); Iwellemmeden WE/WW and N do not; the WE of the Kel-Aghlal accent the antepenult in the simple perfect); Motylinski states on p. 2 that the Hoggar dialect is called tamahaq by its speakers and on p. 6 lists Hoggar, Ifor'as, Adhar', Azger, Ahir and Aoulimiden as differing dialects; Hanoteau's grammar is based on Imouchar' consultants in Algiers in 1858 and is filed under Tahaggart (thv) by the MPI record.

sources.quote: Quant au touareg, les anciens auteurs ne parlent pas de l'accent. Mais Karl-G. Prasse traite le problème de l'accent en touareg dans ses « Notes sur la langue touarègue » (Acta Orientalia, XXV, 1959, p. 43-111). Le même sujet est repris augmenté dans son Manuel de grammaire touarègue, Copenhague, 1972, vol. 1, p. 30-37. [...] Les Touaregs du Hoggar et de l'Aïr disent íkәbrān « huttes », íhănān « tentes » [...] Certains mots sont accentués sur la pénultième : abáyoγ « outre », akátab « écriture ».
sources.note: Second-hand: §7-8 summarize Prasse 1959 (Acta Orientalia 25: 43-111) and Prasse 1972 vol. 1 pp. 30-37 -- three accent degrees, no phonological function, complicated rules, 3-2-1-2-3 rhythm, examples áġənnà 'ciel', some words penult (abáyoġ, akátab), ámis vs səmmús; notes Hoggar/Aïr íkəbrān vs Iwellemmeden ikə́brān.
